title: Tukaram
carry: one for you and one for me

segments.voice: Yesterday, Namdev ran after a dog with the butter, and sang behind a temple until, the story says, it turned to face him. What did you hand over instead of grabbing back? Day nine hundred nineteen.

A man is walking home along a village road with an armful of sugarcane, a gift from a farmer whose field he'd been helping with. Sugarcane is a treat: you peel it and chew it for the sweet juice. Children see him coming and run up. Can we have some? He hands one stalk to the first child. Then one to the next, and the next. By the time he reaches his own door, he's holding a single stalk. Waiting inside is his wife, who has a household to feed. The man is Tukaram, and today we meet him.
screen: `AN ARMFUL OF SUGARCANE.` → `THE CHILDREN ASK.` → `ONE STALK LEFT.`

segments.voice: Tukaram is remembered as a grocer in the village of Dehu, on the Indrayani river. He was a devotee of Vitthal, the same god of Pandharpur that Namdev sang to. Tradition even ties the two together: it says Namdev came to Tukaram in a dream, with Vitthal beside him, and set him the task of making songs. And the songs came. But the stories don't pretend his life was easy. Tradition says his shop failed, that famine hit his region, and that he lost people he loved. Out of that grief, the stories say, he turned his whole life toward Vitthal. Which brings us back to the door, and the one stalk. His wife is waiting, and she's furious. Tradition remembers her as sharp-tongued, but the story is fair to her: the family is poor, and her husband keeps giving everything away. She grabs the last stalk and brings it down across his back. It snaps in two. And Tukaram, rubbing his shoulder, looks at the two pieces and says something like: wonderful, now there's one for you and one for me. You can hear it two ways, and both are true to him. It's funny. It's also a man who has decided, all the way down, that nothing he's handed is really his to hoard, not the cane, not even the moment of being hit. The anger doesn't get a fight back. It gets half the sugarcane. The Varkari tradition he belonged to doesn't ask anyone to leave home for a cave. It holds up people like this: a grocer, a husband, with debts and a hungry household waiting at the door, singing to Vitthal right in the middle of it.
screen: `A GROCER OF DEHU.` · `NAMDEV IN A DREAM.` · `THE STALK SNAPS IN TWO.` · then, large: `ONE FOR YOU AND ONE FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Think of one thing you were handed recently that you didn't fully keep: time, money, attention, patience, that you gave away along the road, maybe before it got to the people at home. Don't scold yourself, and don't defend yourself either. Just notice where it went. Then think of the person waiting at your own door. What's the one stalk you could still split with them today? Let it be something small. If you pray, you can hold both the road and the door before God. The bell holds the time.
Tukaram. The grocer-saint of Dehu who gave away the sugarcane on the road home, and split the last broken stalk with the wife who broke it.
Your line: one for you and one for me. Today, when something breaks in an argument, look for the way to say: one for you and one for me. Day nine hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Tukaram belongs to the Varkari tradition of Maharashtra; Varkaris sing his songs to Vitthal at home and in temples, and the stories of his life are told and retold among them.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man too soft to say no.
what it means: someone who has decided nothing he's handed is his to hoard, not even the moment of being hit.
what a scholar hears: the Varkari saints hold up a householder's devotion, sung in the middle of debts and family life, not away from them.

notes: All paraphrase; nothing quoted. The sugarcane story, the dream of Namdev, the shop's failure and the famine are framed as tradition. Confirm the details, including whether the cane came from a farmer's field he had been guarding or working.
Tukaram's wife (Jijai, also called Avali) is not named; a Keeper may want her named. The script frames her anger as understandable, to avoid making her the butt of the story.
Source: confirm Mahipati's Bhaktalilamrita as the right hagiography to cite for Tukaram's life, or cite Tukaram's own abhangas for the dream.
Original: तुकाराम with stress guide too-kaa-RAAM; a Marathi speaker should confirm the stress.
Editor pass: closing line changed from 'a temper waiting at the door' to 'a hungry household waiting at the door', so the wife is not reduced to her anger at the end.
